container: Media bias shapes how people understand events, institutions, and one another. News outlets choose which stories receive attention, whose voices are included, and what language describes an issue. These decisions can influence public opinion even when reports contain accurate facts. Repeated coverage of crime, for example, may make audiences believe danger is rising, while limited attention to other concerns can make them seem unimportant. Political framing can also encourage viewers to interpret the same policy as either helpful or harmful. Bias does not always result from deliberate deception. Owners, advertisers, audience expectations, newsroom routines, and journalist assumptions can all affect coverage. Social media adds another influence by recommending content that matches users' interests, sometimes creating isolated information bubbles. People may then encounter fewer opposing perspectives and become more certain that their own views are widely shared. Audiences can reduce these effects by comparing reports from varied sources, checking evidence, and distinguishing factual claims from commentary. A fully neutral account may be impossible, but fairness and transparency are achievable goals. When citizens question framing without rejecting trustworthy reporting, they can form more informed opinions and participate more thoughtfully in public life.
